SEC15A-01.convention: 'one of the few X that ___' agreement: strict grammar makes the relative clause agree with the plural 'components' (are), but Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage and Garner record singular agreement with 'one' as established edited usage
SEC15A-01.note: Present tense from 'is one of'; plural because 'that' refers to 'components'. A ('is') is what most edited prose would print after 'The balance spring ... is one of', so the key rests on a disputed usage point the College Board normally avoids.
SEC15A-01.drop_reason: Not exclusive: 'is still shaped' (A) agrees with 'one', which Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage and Garner accept in edited prose, and it is what most writers would print after 'The balance spring ... is one of'. The explanation's strict 'that refers to components' reading is correct, but a test-taker who picks A has a recognised usage authority behind them, which the SAT avoids. Re-author with an antecedent that is not disputed, or remove 'one of'.

SEC15A-02.note: 'For many generations by the time ... arrived in 1896' demands past perfect (progressive). B 'were mining' is the attractive distractor for readers who see only the past setting; C (future perfect) can be dismissed in a historical narrative.

SEC15A-03.note: Head noun 'core' is singular; 'together with dozens of samples' is parenthetical and does not make the subject plural. The following 'that'-clause needs an active verb, so the passive C/D fail; B is the lure for readers who treat 'together with' as 'and'.

SEC15A-04.note: An infinitive phrase ('To reconstruct ... priests') is the singular subject and needs a finite verb, so D. C 'require' is attractive because the plural 'priests' sits right before the blank; A and B leave the sentence with no main verb.

SEC15A-05.note: The antecedent is 'tunnel' (singular), so possessive 'its'. C 'it's' and D 'they're' are contractions that can be rejected on sight, which leaves a plain its/their choice.

SEC15A-06.note: 'both recorded ... and copied' is a correlative pair joining two predicates of one subject, so no punctuation goes before 'and'. B is attractive because the first predicate is long and contains a list; C and D break the both...and pair.

SEC15A-07.note: 'an island whose ...' is an appositive renaming Murano at the end of the sentence, so it takes one comma. B and D leave a fragment after the mark; A runs the noun and its appositive together.

SEC15B-01.note: Plural head 'escapements', with a long gap full of singular nouns (prototype, watchmaker, its drawings), plus 'since 1774', which requires present perfect: D. C 'has kept' is the strongest lure because it gets the tense right and agrees with the nearby singulars.

SEC15B-02.note: The rags were collected 'by itinerant peddlers', so the verb must be past and passive. C 'collected' reads as a participle and leaves no main verb (a fragment), D is active and makes the rags do the collecting, and B is the wrong tense for the 1340s.

SEC15B-03.note: A completed action dated 'in the spring of 1857' takes the simple past. B (present perfect with a specific past date) is the only real distractor; D (future) is obviously wrong in a historical narrative.

SEC15B-04.note: Singular 'silkworm' with a long appositive ending in the plurals 'farmers' and 'groves' needs the finite 'depends'. A is the proximity lure; B and C leave no main verb. Same template and same key letter as A-04.

SEC15B-05.note: The first sentence is a statement with an indirect question ('puzzled over how ...'), so it ends with a period, not a question mark. A is the strong lure; C is a comma splice and D a run-on.

SEC15B-06.note: 'its bronze, alloyed ..., proving too brittle' has no finite verb ('proving' is a participle), so it is an absolute phrase and attaches with a comma. B and C are attractive because 'its bronze' looks like the subject of a new clause, but each leaves a fragment; you only see that by reading on to 'proving'.

SEC15B-07.note: 'drawing water from a single spring' is a restrictive modifier ('Only the households' that drew from it) inside the subject, so it takes no punctuation. A and B open a nonrestrictive interruption that never closes before 'escaped', which splits subject from verb; D puts a colon after a non-clause.

tells: The semicolon is never the key. It appears in A-06, A-07 and B-06 and loses each time; the colon (B-07) also loses.

Semicolon/period twins: A-07 and B-06 offer both '; X' and '. X', which are interchangeable between independent clauses. A test-taker who reasons that both cannot be right strikes both and is left with a two-way choice (A-07: A/C; B-06: A/D). A-06 offers the near-twins '; and' / '. And', which works the same way.

Boundary items whose key is no punctuation (A-06, B-07) or a single comma (A-07, B-06): the plainest option or the lightest mark wins in 4 of the 5 non-terminal punctuation items. Only B-05 is keyed to a full stop.

Agreement items always print the proximity lure (the verb agreeing with the nearest noun) as a distractor, and the key is always the verb that agrees with the distant head noun (A-03, A-04, B-01, B-04). A student who learns to 'pick the agreement that does NOT match the noun right before the blank' answers all four without finding the subject. A-01 breaks the pattern only because its key is itself contested.
Non-finite distractors (-ing, to + verb) lose every time they appear (A-04, B-04), so they can be struck without parsing the sentence.
Key letters are balanced (A 4, B 3, C 3, D 4); there is no slot tell.
summary.near_duplicate_notes: A-04/B-04: same option shape (-ing / to + verb / plural / singular -s), a singular subject followed by plural nouns, and the same key letter D. A-03/B-04/B-01: a long noun phrase whose distant head noun decides agreement. A-01/B-01: 2x2 grids crossing number with tense or aspect. A-02/B-03: tense fixed by a dated past anchor. A-07/B-06: a comma key with semicolon and period twins offered. A-06/B-07: no-punctuation keys that hold a structure together (both...and; a restrictive modifier inside the subject).

phase2_note: All 14 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses), and every explanation reaches its key and rejects each distractor for a correct reason. I recommend dropping one item: A-01, for the disputed 'one of the ... that' agreement. Not item-level drops, but worth fixing at batch level: A-04 and B-04 are one template with the same option shape and key letter, so keep only one. A-05 and B-03 are easy with weak distractors, below the module-2 hard target. The semicolon never wins and the semicolon/period twins in A-07 and B-06 (plus '; and' / '. And' in A-06) allow two-option elimination. The agreement items all reward 'avoid the verb that matches the nearest noun'.
